Chain merges are marked by a first-class merged_from edge whose source is the first version of the successor chain and whose target is the terminal version of each predecessor chain. Chains are not first-class graph nodes; merged_from is an ordinary edge whose semantics express chain-level provenance. On merge, predecessor edges are tombstoned by setting valid_until_version on the edge at the terminal predecessor version; edges on the successor chain must be explicitly re-attached through tooling that surfaces predecessor edges for review. Auto-migration is forbidden. The meta-edges supersedes, retracts, and merged_from all carry resolution_policy: none. They are version-specific facts about lineage state, not relationships that propagate through it. The supersedes operation remains edge-free with respect to outbound edges on the superseded version: sage_ingest with supersedes_document_id does not propagate outbound edges forward, and the resolver performs inheritance walks at query time using the anchor and retraction primitives. sage_traverse is modified to consult the edge-type registry during chain walks and to honor anchor and retraction semantics.
adrs.rationale: The chain-versus-version distinction is real and load-bearing. Relationships that persist across version turnover should be expressed as chain-to-chain edges with declared resolution policy, keeping the graph's edge count proportional to semantic relationships rather than to version cardinality. Anchoring via a document_id chain member, rather than a wall-clock timestamp, is robust to backfills, replays, and clock skew. First-class retraction edges preserve audit trails and support time-travel queries, which mutation-based approaches cannot. Anchoring retractions at the successor version, rather than the predecessor, matches the mental model that retraction takes effect going forward. Two separate nullable anchor fields, rather than a tuple-valued field, is the right schema shape for five reinforcing reasons. Uniform schema: every edge row has the same columns regardless of resolution_policy, so the resolver, traversal API, validators, and debug tooling read the relevant field directly without branching to interpret the schema. Standard null semantics: a null source_valid_from_version on a transitive_target edge is not a special case but a declaration of 'not applicable,' handled natively by every storage layer. Queryability: predicates like 'find all edges whose source anchor is a chain member of X' are indexed column queries; tuple variants would degrade into JSON blobs (losing indexability) or composite types (awkward for query planners). Policy evolution: adding a new resolution_policy in the future is schema-additive rather than schema-invasive; tuple variants would force reinterpretation of existing rows. Validator simplicity: the write-time invariant becomes a declarative table lookup from policy to required fields, enforced at the edge-write boundary rather than caught later by the resolver. Two distinct retraction mechanisms exist because they reflect different causes. In-chain retractions are governance events: a steward or agent decides that a relationship no longer holds from some version forward, and that decision is itself an auditable fact worth preserving as a first-class edge. Merge-triggered tombstones are mechanical consequences of a chain-topology operation; no separate governance act is occurring. Collapsing both into a single valid_until_version mechanism would lose the distinction between deliberate retraction and structural termination. Chain identity is kept implicit (via document_id through supersedes lineage) to avoid a schema addition whose benefit is marginal in the expected use pattern. Representing chain merges as first-class merged_from edges (rather than a marker on the terminal supersede) keeps chain lineage queryable, generalizes to forks, and cleanly separates version-level succession (supersedes) from chain-level provenance (merged_from). Requiring explicit re-attachment on merge converts a silent-inheritance hazard into a review checkpoint: the new chain's coverage may be a superset, subset, or reorganization of its predecessors, and the architecture should not assume any of the three. Worked example illustrating interval composition. Consider two chains: chain A with versions a1 through a9 and chain B with versions b1 through b5. At time T1, a covers edge with resolution_policy transitive_both is introduced between the chains, with source_valid_from_version = a3 and target_valid_from_version = b2. A query at (a5, b3) resolves to the edge: a5 is downstream of a3, b3 is downstream of b2, no retraction exists. At time T2, a retracts edge is introduced targeting the covers edge, anchored on chain A at a7. A query at (a8, b4) locates the covers edge during the walk, detects the retraction anchored at a7 (upstream of a8), and short-circuits; the edge does not surface. A query at (a6, b3) locates the covers edge and detects no retraction upstream of a6; the edge surfaces. At time T3, chain A is superseded into a new chain C via merge; a merged_from edge is attached from c1 to a9, and the covers edge's valid_until_version is set to a9. A query starting from c2 does not find the covers edge on chain A (it terminates at a9), and no covers edge on chain C exists until someone explicitly re-attaches one. This composition is the full set of interactions the resolver must handle. The merged_from edge type is substrate-level infrastructure. No immediate operational need forces its implementation. It is included now for shape coherence: the anchor and retraction primitives compose correctly only if the chain-topology operations are treated as first-class primitives at the same layer. Designing merged_from when the first merge occurs would either force a retrofitted change to established schemas or admit a silent-inheritance hazard for the first merge event.
consequences: SAGE's edge schema gains source_valid_from_version and target_valid_from_version, both nullable document_id references, plus valid_until_version (nullable) used exclusively for merge-triggered tombstoning.

A write-time validator enforces the invariant that populated anchor fields match resolution_policy: transitive_source requires source only, transitive_target requires target only, transitive_both requires both, none forbids both. Violations are refused at the edge-write boundary.

The edge-type registry lives in SAGE core and gains a resolution_policy field with an enumerated type over {transitive_source, transitive_target, transitive_both, none}. The meta-edges supersedes, retracts, and merged_from all carry resolution_policy: none.

Two new edge types are introduced: retracts (governance-level edge retraction, anchored on the retracting chain, targeting the retracted edge instance) and merged_from (chain-level provenance, source at the first version of the successor chain, target at the terminal version of each predecessor).

sage_traverse is modified to consult the edge-type registry and honor anchor and retraction semantics during chain walks. Its return shape gains a resolution_path field, populated under a debug flag, exposing the edge instances consulted, the anchors evaluated, and any retractions applied during resolution.

sage_ingest with supersedes_document_id remains edge-free with respect to outbound edges on the superseded version: edges are not propagated at ingest time. The resolver performs inheritance walks at query time.

Existing edges require a one-time migration to populate anchor fields. For transitive_source edges, source_valid_from_version is set to the edge's source document_id (the edge becomes valid as of the version at which it was attached) and target_valid_from_version remains null; the mirror policy applies to transitive_target. No other edge data is touched.
Chain merges require tooling that surfaces predecessor edges for review on the successor chain and proposes re-attachments. Auto-migration is explicitly forbidden.

Performance envelope: transitive_both edges over chains accumulating many versions incur compounding chain-walk cost at query time. The resolver MAY cache per-chain-head edge sets with invalidation on supersedes ingest, retracts ingest, or merged_from ingest. Cache design is deferred to implementation; the ADR establishes that caching is expected but not normatively specified.

The Formal Substrate edge schema documents the four-valued resolution_policy enumeration, the source_valid_from_version / target_valid_from_version / valid_until_version field semantics, the retracts and merged_from edge types, and the write-time invariant. The Formal Substrate manifest updates to reflect these additions.
Time-travel queries become expressible: historical edge state at any version is recoverable through anchor and retraction markers without mutating current edges.
Chain-to-chain edges are attached once at relationship instantiation and otherwise untouched; routine version advancement does not touch the edge table.

An error-recovery procedure for re-pointing a supersedes edge (the rare case where a document is reassigned to a different chain) is documented separately and requires re-evaluation of edges whose anchor fields reference the reassigned document_id. Implicit chain identity otherwise remains uncompromised.

adrs.title: Ingestion is exclusively intentional; SAGE provides no file watcher or auto-ingest
adrs.context: The SAGE source_adapters schema carried a watch_paths property on each adapter's config, and prose in the SAGE Architecture Reference (Source Change Detection) and Deployment Model described a file watcher as a SAGE capability. No code ever consumed the field: there is no watcher process, no polling loop, no scheduled scan, and no consumer of watch_paths anywhere in the SAGE source tree. The schema slot and the prose were forward declarations for a capability that was never built and that, on review, is not wanted. Source files have a life independent of SAGE; the system records provenance at ingestion and detects change on re-ingestion via content-hash comparison. Adding a watcher would expand SAGE's surface from a request-response state substrate to a long-running observer of the user's file system, with all the operational consequences that entails (process supervision, cross-platform watcher implementations, cloud-sync filesystem races, security posture for file-event subscription, surprise ingestion of files the user did not intend to commit to the canonical record).

options_considered.option: Implement the file watcher described in the architecture
options_considered.summary: Build a watcher process per vault that monitors watch_paths, detects file create / modify / delete events, and triggers ingest or re-ingest automatically. Provide a polling fallback for paths the watcher cannot observe.
pros: Matches the prose in the SAGE Architecture Reference as written
Removes the manual step of invoking ingest after dropping a file
cons: Expands SAGE from request-response to long-running observer; introduces process-supervision concerns
Cross-platform watcher implementations differ (inotify, FSEvents, ReadDirectoryChangesW) and degrade on cloud-sync filesystems
Auto-ingest removes the user's intentional act of committing a file to the canonical record; files appear in the graph as a side effect of saving them
Watcher events fire mid-write; debouncing logic adds complexity and can still racewith partial-write states
Security posture: a watcher subscribing to file events sees more than what it ingests, including names of files the user never intended to expose

options_considered.option: Leave watch_paths in the schema as a forward declaration
options_considered.summary: Keep the field in the schema as a documented intent, even though no code reads it.
pros: No churn to the schema, vault configs, or contract tests
cons: Schema-as-contract is undermined when published fields have no implementation
Vault authors who populate watch_paths reasonably expect it to do something
Drift between contract and code accumulates; the next reader has to relitigate the question

options_considered.option: Remove watch_paths and formalize the intentional-ingestion constraint (chosen)
options_considered.summary: Strip watch_paths from the source_adapters schema, vault configs, and contract-test fixtures. Establish as an architectural constraint that documents enter SAGE only through an explicit MCP tool or API call (sage_ingest, app_scan_directory + app_batch_ingest). Source change detection happens only when a caller invokes ingest on a known path; SAGE then re-runs the adapter, hash-compares, and supersedes if changed.
pros: Schema and code agree on what SAGE actually does
Ingestion remains a deliberate, auditable act by a caller (human via the application, agent via MCP)
SAGE stays a request-response state substrate with no long-running observer surface
Cross-platform behavior is determined by the caller's directory walk, not by a per-OS watcher implementation
Cloud-sync filesystem semantics, partial-write races, and file-event security posture become non-issues
cons: Adding files to a vault requires the user (or an agent) to explicitly trigger a scan / ingest; no passive ingestion of file-drops
The SAGE Architecture Reference's Source Change Detection section and the Deployment Model's indexing row are out of date and require revision when those documents are next updated

adrs.decision: SAGE does not implement file watching, polling, scheduled scans, or any other form of auto-ingest. Documents enter SAGE only when a caller explicitly invokes an ingest operation: sage_ingest for a single document, or app_scan_directory followed by app_batch_ingest for bulk paths. Source change detection is tied to that explicit invocation: when a caller re-ingests a known path, SAGE re-runs the source adapter, compares the new content_hash against the stored source_content_hash, and creates a supersedes-linked successor document if they differ. The watch_paths property is removed from the source_adapters schema. Vault configs that carried it are migrated to drop the field. The SAGE Architecture Reference's Source Change Detection section and the Deployment Model's indexing row are flagged as stale and will be revised in their next pass; this ADR is the authoritative statement of the constraint until then.
adrs.rationale: SAGE's architectural identity is a request-response state substrate. Ingestion that happens as a side effect of the user's filesystem activity is incompatible with that identity in three ways. First, it shifts the trust boundary: with explicit ingest, the caller commits the file; with a watcher, the file commits itself and the user finds out later. The caller's intentional act is the auditable signal that something belongs in the canonical record. Second, it shifts the operational footprint: a watcher requires SAGE to be a long-running process with per-vault subscriptions, cross-platform event handling, and recovery semantics for missed events; the request-response model has no such requirements. Third, it shifts the failure mode: with a watcher, partial writes, swap-file activity from editors, and cloud-sync transients all become candidate ingestion events that the watcher must filter out or debounce; with explicit ingest, the caller chooses the moment when the file is in a known-good state. The CAS Application's directory-scan workflow already provides the convenience that watching would offer (drop files into a directory, then click Scan), without any of these costs. Removing watch_paths rather than leaving it as a forward declaration enforces the principle that the schema is the contract: published fields must have implementations behind them. This is the second instance in the system where a forward-declared schema field would have been better not declared (the first was source_references in the manifest, removed in Formal Substrate v0.1).
consequences: sage/source_adapters.schema.json drops the watch_paths property; the file_extensions description is updated to refer to directory scans and bulk ingestion rather than 'the file watcher'.

Live vault configs that reference watch_paths are cleaned up. The pim_health vault (the only live vault carrying the field) has its three adapter entries (docx, markdown, xlsx) stripped of watch_paths.
Contract-test fixtures in tests/sage/contract_tests.md are revised to drop watch_paths from the example YAML; no test count or assertion change.

The SAGE Architecture Reference's 'Source Change Detection' section (currently describes a file watcher as capability #2 alongside provenance and versioned re-ingestion) is stale. Source change detection occurs only on caller-initiated re-ingest, comparing new content_hash to the stored source_content_hash and creating a supersedes-linked successor if they differ. Provenance capture (capability #1) and versioned re-ingestion (capability #3) are unchanged.
The Deployment Model's Phase 1 / Phase 2 indexing row ('Incremental, file-watcher or on-demand') is stale. Indexing is on-demand only, in both phases.
SAGE's runtime surface remains request-response. No watcher processes, no per-vault long-running subscriptions, no platform-specific filesystem-event integration code is in scope.
Future reintroduction of file watching, if ever desired, requires a superseding ADR. The constraint is not a deferred design question; it is a positive architectural choice.

adrs.title: Auto edge inference may delete its own prior edges to repair chains; hand-curated edges are protected by a provenance gate
adrs.context: Bulk ingest auto edge inference (app/backend/edge_inference.py) groups documents by (title, project, doc_type) and emits a linear supersedes chain sorted by normalized version. Within a single batch this works regardless of arrival order — the engine sorts before chaining. Across batches it does not. Two reinforcing constraints in the prior implementation produced incorrect chains when a version arrived later than its successor: (1) the engine fetched only active documents from the vault, so a previously-superseded predecessor was invisible to subsequent inference passes; (2) the engine added new edges but never removed stale ones. Concrete failure: ingest v1 in batch 1 (active), ingest v3 in batch 2 (engine sees v1 active, emits v3→v1, archives v1), ingest v2 in batch 3 (engine sees v3 active and v1 archived/hidden, emits v3→v2, archives v2). Result: v3 has two outbound supersedes edges (→ v1 and → v2), the v2→v1 edge is missing, and the chain is forked rather than linear. Fixing this requires the engine to compute the desired chain against the full historical chain (including archived predecessors) and emit edge removals as well as adds. That capability raises a question with architectural weight: should auto inference be allowed to delete edges it did not create? The supersedes graph carries both auto-inferred edges (from filename version detection) and hand-curated edges (created via the link operation by a human reviewer or an agent acting on a reviewer's behalf). The two have different epistemic status: auto-inferred edges are mechanical conclusions from filename metadata that the engine can re-derive at any time; hand-curated edges encode reviewer judgment that the engine has no way to reproduce. A chain-repair operation that conflates them risks silently overwriting reviewer judgment with mechanical inference, which is the opposite of the intended trust direction (humans correct the engine; the engine does not correct humans). The decision must establish where chain repair sits on the auto/manual authority spectrum without giving up the bug fix.

options_considered.option: Always stage chain-repair edge removals as Tier 2 (conservative)
options_considered.summary: Whenever chain repair would remove an existing edge, emit the proposed adds + removals as Tier 2 staging entries regardless of how the existing edge was authored. The human reviewer approves the repair in the staging UI; the engine never deletes a production edge automatically.
pros: No edge deletion happens without explicit human approval; the manual-curation invariant is absolute
Uniform behavior — reviewers do not have to reason about provenance
Aligns with the existing two-tier model where the reviewer is the only mutation authority for ambiguous decisions
cons: The most common chain-repair case (engine fixing a chain it built itself) becomes a manual review task; 'ingest in any order, get the right chain' is no longer automatic
Reviewer queue fills with mechanical fix-ups that have no judgment content; risk of approval fatigue degrading the value of staging review
The reviewer cannot easily distinguish 'engine repairing its own work' from 'engine proposing to overwrite my work' — both look like Tier 2 supersedes proposals in the queue

options_considered.option: Always auto-repair as Tier 1 (aggressive)
options_considered.summary: Treat the supersedes chain as a derived, mechanical structure: chain identity (title, project, doc_type) is invariant, order is deterministic from normalized version. Whenever the existing chain disagrees with the desired chain, the engine corrects it automatically — adds missing edges and removes stale ones, regardless of how the existing edges were authored.
pros: Out-of-order ingestion always converges to the correct chain with no human intervention
Treats the supersedes graph as a true derived view of filename metadata, simplifying the mental model
No new schema or rationale conventions required
cons: Can silently delete hand-curated edges; a reviewer who manually attached v3 directly to v1 (perhaps because v2 was an aborted draft) loses that edge as soon as v2 is later ingested with the same chain identity
Reverses the trust direction: the engine corrects the human rather than the human correcting the engine
No record of the deletion is visible to the reviewer until they notice the missing edge; loss of curated state is silent
Would require either tombstoning deleted edges or a separate audit log to make the deletion recoverable; both add architectural surface

options_considered.option: Provenance-gated repair: auto only when removed edges were themselves auto-inferred (chosen)
options_considered.summary: Stamp every auto-inferred chain edge with a recognizable rationale signature ('[version_chain]' prefix on the rationale field). Chain repair computes the desired chain and the diff against existing edges as before. If every edge in a group's removal set carries the version_chain signature, the repair executes as Tier 1: removals via graph_ops_service.unlink, adds via graph_ops_service.link, lifecycle side effects unchanged. If any edge in the removal set lacks the signature (i.e. is hand-curated), the entire group's repair is downgraded to Tier 2 staging: the proposed new edges are inserted into staging_edges for human review, and the conflicting hand-curated edge is left untouched in the production graph.
pros: Common case is automatic: the engine repairing a chain it built itself requires no human intervention
Hand-curated edges are never silently deleted; the reviewer's judgment is preserved by default
Trust direction is preserved: the engine corrects its own prior conclusions but defers to human judgment when the two disagree
Provenance signal is local to the rationale field; no separate edge table or audit log is required

Group-level (not edge-level) gate: if any part of a chain group has a hand-curated edge, the entire group's repair stages, so the reviewer sees the full proposed picture in one place rather than receiving a mix of auto and staged changes within the same chain
cons: Two policies operate side by side; reviewers must understand why some chain repairs appear in staging and others do not
Pre-existing edges in live vaults lack the version_chain rationale prefix; until those chains are touched and replanned, every chain repair against legacy data downgrades to Tier 2 staging
The rationale field carries a structural signal (the prefix) in addition to its human-readable content; future changes to rationale formatting must preserve the prefix or update the recognition logic

adrs.decision: Auto edge inference may delete supersedes edges it previously created in order to repair a chain when an out-of-order arrival inserts an intermediate version. Recognition is by rationale prefix: edges authored by version_chain inference carry a leading '[version_chain]' marker on the rationale field, set at creation time in app/backend/edge_inference.py. Chain repair operates per chain-identity group ((title.lower(), project, doc_type)). For each group with a new versioned arrival, the engine computes the desired sorted chain, diffs it against existing supersedes edges between group members, and produces a candidate set of adds and removals. If every edge in the candidate removal set carries the version_chain rationale prefix, the repair executes as Tier 1 (immediate): removals are processed first via graph_ops_service.unlink, then adds via graph_ops_service.link, and the existing lifecycle side effect on Tier 1 supersedes adds (transition target to archived) fires as before. If any edge in the candidate removal set lacks the prefix, the entire group's repair is downgraded to Tier 2: the proposed new edges are emitted as staging_edges entries for human review, the candidate removals are dropped from the executed plan, and the hand-curated edges remain in the production graph untouched. The downgrade is group-level, not edge-level, so the human reviewer sees the complete proposed repair in one staging context rather than a partially-applied half-state. The IngestSummary surface gains an edges_removed counter (also surfaced in to_dict) so callers can observe when chain-repair removals occurred.
adrs.rationale: The supersedes graph carries two epistemically distinct kinds of edges: mechanical conclusions from filename version metadata (which the engine can re-derive at any time) and reviewer judgments (which the engine cannot reproduce). The right policy is to let the engine update its own prior conclusions while protecting reviewer judgments by default. This preserves the trust direction the system depends on elsewhere — humans correct the engine; the engine does not silently correct humans. The rationale-prefix mechanism is the smallest architectural surface that makes the distinction recordable and recognizable: the rationale field already exists, already carries a human-readable explanation, and is already the place where edge provenance information naturally lives. A separate created_by_method field would have been more explicit but would have required a schema migration of the edges table, with no operational benefit beyond the prefix scheme. Group-level downgrade (rather than per-edge mixed application) reflects the observation that a chain is a coherent structure: applying part of a repair while leaving the rest for human review produces a chain that is neither the prior state nor the desired state, which is worse than either. Putting the entire group in front of the reviewer when any part of it is contested gives the reviewer one decision to make rather than several partially-coupled ones. The conservative behavior on legacy edges (chain repair against a vault whose existing chain edges predate the prefix convention will downgrade to Tier 2) is acceptable: the worst outcome is that the reviewer sees a staging proposal where they would have preferred an automatic execution. The opposite error — silently deleting a legacy hand-curated edge because the recognition logic cannot tell it apart from an auto edge — is not recoverable without an audit log this system does not maintain.
consequences: Edges authored by version_chain inference now carry a '[version_chain] ' prefix on the rationale field. The recognition function _is_version_chain_edge in app/backend/edge_inference.py checks rationale.startswith(VERSION_CHAIN_RATIONALE_PREFIX); future edge-rationale formatting changes must preserve the prefix or update the recognition logic in lockstep.

EdgePlan in app/backend/edge_inference.py gains a removals: list[PlannedEdgeRemoval] field. resolve_and_execute processes removals before adds so chain-repair leaves no transient invalid state visible to the lifecycle side effect that fires on Tier 1 adds.

EdgeResult and IngestSummary gain an edges_removed: int counter, also surfaced via IngestSummary.to_dict(). Both MCP (app_batch_ingest) and FastAPI (POST /app/ingest) callers emit the new field; downstream consumers (the React app's Ingest results panel) need to tolerate it.

_build_edge_plan in app/backend/ingest_service.py now (a) includes archived documents whose chain identity matches a new versioned arrival and (b) pre-fetches existing supersedes edges between those chain-scope members. This is the only place where archived documents participate in auto edge inference; the prior 'active only' rule still applies to non-chain-repair inference.

Pre-existing supersedes edges in live vaults lack the [version_chain] prefix and will therefore be treated as hand-curated by the provenance gate. The first chain-repair operation that would touch a legacy edge downgrades the entire group's repair to Tier 2 staging. This is intentional: legacy edges may be hand-curated, and there is no safe way to distinguish them retroactively. Vault owners who want chain repair to operate at Tier 1 against legacy data must re-author the affected chains so the new edges carry the prefix.

The CAS Application's staging review surface (Review tab) currently presents Tier 2 supersedes proposals as standalone edge suggestions. Chain-repair proposals are structurally different: they propose a new edge that conflicts with an existing edge in the production graph. The staging UI does not yet surface this conflict context; the reviewer sees the proposed new edge but is not shown the existing edge it would replace. A follow-on UX change is needed so the reviewer can see and act on both sides of the conflict in one place. Until that change lands, reviewers approving chain-repair staging entries should also manually inspect and unlink the conflicting hand-curated edge if the repair is correct.

Test coverage for chain repair lives in tests/app/test_batch_ingest_service.py (TestChainRepair, TEST-CR-001 through TEST-CR-005), with an in-memory _MockGraphState that backs the GraphStore and GraphOpsService surfaces the planner uses. The Test Plan version note should be updated to reflect the new test scope when next bumped.

Future expansion of auto edge inference to other edge types (covers, depends_on, etc.) inherits the provenance-prefix convention: any edge type that gains an automatic creator must stamp its rationale with a recognizable prefix and check it before any deletion.

adrs.title: Abstract generation prompt: descriptive framing for agent relevance triage
adrs.context: ADR-011 establishes that semantic abstracts are generated at ingestion and stored on the document record. It does not address how the generation prompt should be shaped. Two facts about the abstract's runtime context now make the prompt design architectural rather than implementation detail. First, the abstract's purpose is agent relevance triage: an autonomous agent that has discovered the document via an MCP discovery tool (sage_discover, sage_traverse) reads the abstract to decide whether to fetch the full document. The agent already sees title, doc_type, tags, project, lifecycle_status, and document_date in the same payload, so the abstract must carry what those fields cannot -- what the document is about, what it claims or prescribes, and what it covers. Second, abstract generation runs under greedy decoding (temperature 0.0), per the determinism property tested by TEST-SAGE-AD-029. Determinism is the right choice for reproducibility and governance, but it has a corollary: when a prompt-source pair has a pathological attractor for any expected document class, that pathology reproduces identically on every re-run. The original prompt ('You are a technical abstraction engine. Given the full text of a document, produce a concise semantic abstract that captures the key concepts, methods, and findings.') was research-paper-shaped and document-type-blind. Empirical investigation of seven editorial-guideline documents in the theology vault documented four failure modes: (1) genre-instantiation, where prescriptive documents about a writing genre produce specimens of that genre rather than descriptions of the prescription; (2) hypothetical-paper composition, where a guideline about academic theology becomes the abstract of an invented paper on divine silence; (3) fabricated specifics, where a guideline about executive communications produces an abstract containing an invented $120,000 budget reallocation with fabricated percentages and dates; (4) framing-tax openings, where the master Editorial Guidelines document opens with three sentences of generic AI-discourse boilerplate before reaching content. Only the shortest, most instruction-dense source (Social Media) escaped these patterns.

options_considered.option: Status quo: single generic technical-abstract prompt
options_considered.summary: Keep the prompt as-is; treat the failures as model limitations.
pros: Zero implementation change
Preserves a single uniform prompt across all document types
cons: The four failure modes are reproducible and architectural, not transient model artifacts
The Church Leadership case (fabricated $120,000 reallocation) is a factual-safety failure, not a quality issue
Determinism guarantees the pathology persists across re-runs

options_considered.option: Switch to sampling (temperature > 0) to introduce variance
options_considered.summary: Replace greedy decoding with low-temperature sampling so re-runs produce different outputs.
pros: Some runs would land in non-pathological output regions
cons: Masks the prompt problem rather than fixing it
Breaks the reproducibility property tested by TEST-SAGE-AD-029
Stored abstracts become non-deterministic relative to source, complicating debugging and governance
A prompt that has bad attractors at temperature 0 still has them at temperature 0.7; sampling just rolls dice across them

options_considered.option: Per-doc-type prompt overrides via vault config
options_considered.summary: Allow each vault's configuration to specify per-doc-type prompt templates.
pros: Maximum flexibility for domain-specific prompts
cons: Heavier than the documented failures require
Multiplies prompts to maintain and test as new doc_types emerge
The keystone fix (descriptive framing) is uniform across all doc_types; the per-type signal is captured by passing doc_type into a single template

options_considered.option: Two-pass abstraction with self-critique
options_considered.summary: Generate, then have the model critique its own output against the doc-vs-genre rule, then revise.
pros: Could catch failures the first pass misses
cons: Violates the standing principle on planning-then-execution separation: post-completion self-evaluation is a known failure mode
Doubles the inference cost per document
Does not address the root cause (prompt shape); adds a layer that may itself drift

options_considered.option: Descriptive third-person prompt with doc_type parameter and explicit anti-fabrication clause
options_considered.summary: Reframe the prompt around the abstract's purpose (agent relevance triage), require descriptive third-person voice, surface doc_type to the model, forbid composing in the genre the document discusses, forbid introducing specifics not in the source, and instruct against restating metadata the agent already sees.
pros: Descriptive third-person framing makes genre-instantiation grammatically impossible: the abstract cannot open with a sample pastoral letter when it must open with 'This document...'
doc_type lets the model choose appropriate descriptive verbs (prescribes, argues, narrates, defines) without per-type prompt variants
The no-fabrication clause directly addresses the highest-risk failure (invented specifics in authoritative-looking abstracts)
Aligns the prompt with the abstract's actual consumer (the discovering agent) and the visible discovery-surface metadata
Single template, single call, retains greedy decoding and the TEST-SAGE-AD-029 determinism property
Empirical A/B against the seven editorial-guideline documents eliminated all four failure modes including the fabricated-budget case
cons: Adds doc_type as a required parameter on AbstractionProvider.generate_abstract, requiring an interface change and threading through the ingestion service
Re-abstracting existing documents requires either bulk reabstract or accepting a mixed corpus during transition

adrs.decision: The system prompt for semantic abstract generation must (a) frame the task as producing a relevance-triage card for an agent that has discovered the document via search; (b) require descriptive third-person framing ('This document...', 'The guideline...', 'The text...'); (c) receive the document's doc_type as a parameterized input substituted into the prompt; (d) forbid writing in the voice, style, or genre the document discusses; (e) forbid introducing specifics (numbers, names, dates, quotes, examples) not present in the source text; (f) instruct against restating metadata (title, doc_type, tags, project) that the agent sees alongside the abstract in MCP tool responses; (g) preserve the density-proportional length behavior established by ADR-011. The AbstractionProvider.generate_abstract interface gains a doc_type: str | None parameter, threaded from the document record through the ingestion service to the provider.
adrs.rationale: The abstract's runtime context -- visible alongside doc_type and other metadata to a discovering agent who is using the abstract to triage relevance -- narrows the prompt design space considerably. The agent does not need a miniature replica of the document or a research-paper abstract; it needs a description of what the document is and contains. Descriptive third-person framing is the keystone because it operates structurally rather than by enumeration: a model instructed to begin with 'This document...' cannot grammatically produce a sample pastoral letter, devotional opening, op-ed lede, or hypothetical paper abstract. The doc_type signal disambiguates meta-documents from specimens (a guideline about pastoral writing versus a pastoral letter) without requiring per-type prompt variants. The no-fabrication clause is the necessary supplement because descriptive prose can still hallucinate specifics. Together, the three constraints close all four failure modes documented in the seven-document A/B. The decision to keep greedy decoding (TEST-SAGE-AD-029) unchanged is deliberate: determinism is correct for reproducibility and governance, and the right response to a deterministic system with a bad attractor is to fix the attractor at the prompt design level, not to introduce sampling noise.
consequences: AbstractionProvider.generate_abstract gains a required doc_type: str | None parameter. The Qwen3 implementation and all stub implementations are updated. The interface change is reflected in the formal substrate.

IngestionService threads doc_type from the Document record through _generate_abstract_text, _stage3_abstraction, _run_background_pipeline, and _reabstract_background to the provider. Both the initial-ingest and reabstract code paths pass doc_type.
The system prompt is template-substituted at call time with the doc_type clause. doc_type=None omits the clause cleanly.

TEST-SAGE-AD-029 (deterministic output under greedy decoding) is preserved unchanged. The determinism property is now relied upon by this ADR's argument: prompt design must close all expected attractors because re-runs will not vary.

Empirical validation: the seven editorial-guideline documents in the theology vault (Pastoral, Blog/Devotional, Public Writing, Church Leadership/Executive, Academic Theology, Editorial Guidelines master, Social Media) were re-abstracted in-process. All four prior failure modes -- genre-instantiation, hypothetical-paper composition, fabricated specifics, framing-tax openings -- were eliminated. The Social Media control remained clean.
Stored abstracts under the old prompt are not automatically migrated. Re-abstraction of existing documents is an operational decision (per-vault, on demand via sage_reabstract).

Per-doc-type prompt overrides remain available as future work if a doc_type emerges where the descriptive third-person framing is structurally inappropriate. The current single-template design covers the documented cases.

adrs.title: Metadata inference and review are caller responsibilities; SAGE accepts authoritative values
adrs.context: Two related symptoms surfaced in the same session and resolve to a single boundary problem. Symptom one: an agent ingest of ChecklistTemplate v3.2 (which supersedes v3.1.2 with doc_type=steering_template) produced doc_type=reference_document on the new version, requiring a manual sage_update_metadata correction. Investigation showed that SAGE's ingest pipeline (sage/services/ingestion.py) infers doc_type from filename pattern rules in the vault config (sage/services/filename_parser.py) and never consults the predecessor's doc_type even when supersedes_document_id is supplied. Symptom two: routine agent ingests via the SAGE MCP toolset are appearing in the CAS application's bulk-ingest review queue. Investigation showed that the review queue is the SAGE pending_metadata feed (sage/api/routers/pending_metadata.py), populated whenever the vault config sets metadata_extraction.review_required=true. The CAS application consumes that feed but does not own it. Both symptoms trace to the same boundary leak: SAGE is performing inference and review-queue management on behalf of callers who, in the agent case, already have authoritative metadata. The two standing principles that bear directly: principle 4 (SAGE indexes everything and owns nothing) implies that vault-specific filename heuristics -- which encode caller opinions about how filenames map to metadata -- are out of place in SAGE; principle 5 (boundary rule) places caller-side concerns above SAGE. The bulk-ingest review feature is correct in concept and the CAS application's bulk-ingest UI is functioning correctly; only the implementation placement is wrong. All agents currently using SAGE go through the SAGE MCP toolset, so the caller-side surface to update is bounded.

options_considered.option: Status quo with chain inheritance only
options_considered.summary: Leave filename inference and the auto-populated review queue inside SAGE. Add only the narrow fix: when supersedes_document_id is present and the caller omits doc_type, inherit the predecessor's doc_type.
pros: Smallest possible code change
Resolves the immediate doc_type regression
cons: Does not address the review-queue pollution; agent ingests continue to land in the CAS application's review list
Leaves the boundary leak in place; principle 4 violation persists
Two related symptoms get one fix; the second symptom resurfaces under any future inference rule

options_considered.option: Per-vault default-to-review with caller override
options_considered.summary: Keep review_required as a vault config switch but allow callers to override it per-call. Filename inference continues to run inside SAGE.
pros: Backward compatible with existing vault configs
Lets agents opt out of review per call
cons: Inference still lives in SAGE; principle 4 violation only partially addressed
The same vault sees both authoritative agent ingests and uncertain bulk-ingest uploads; per-vault default is the wrong granularity. Per-call is the right one
Two configuration surfaces (vault config + per-call flag) interact and must be reasoned about together

options_considered.option: Hard reject on doc_type divergence across a supersedes edge
options_considered.summary: Refuse the ingest when the inferred doc_type disagrees with the predecessor's doc_type unless the caller passes an explicit override flag.
pros: No silent mistakes on chain extensions
Forces every doc_type transition to be deliberate
cons: Adds a new failure mode to a forgiving pipeline
Treats inference as authoritative enough to gate ingest; the underlying problem is that inference should not be running for authoritative callers in the first place
Does not address the review-queue pollution

options_considered.option: SAGE accepts authoritative values; inference and review become caller responsibilities; chain inheritance retained as a graph-state exception (chosen)
options_considered.summary: Add a needs_review boolean to IngestRequest, defaulting to false. When false, SAGE commits caller values as-is and does not invoke filename inference. When true, SAGE marks metadata_confirmed=false and the document appears in pending_metadata. FilenameParser remains as a SAGE-provided library, exposed via a new parse_filename endpoint and MCP tool that callers invoke before ingest if they want filename-based suggestions. One exception is retained inside SAGE: when supersedes_document_id is present and the caller omits doc_type, project, or authority_scope, the new document inherits the missing value(s) from the predecessor on a per-field basis. Caller-supplied values continue to win. The vault config option metadata_extraction.review_required is deprecated and removed once the CAS application is updated to pass needs_review=true explicitly.
pros: Resolves both symptoms with one architectural decision: chain inheritance fixes the doc_type regression; needs_review=false default removes the review-queue pollution for agent callers
Aligns implementation with the standing principles: SAGE owns graph state (chain context); callers own caller-side opinions (filename heuristics)
Per-call granularity matches the actual decision boundary: the same vault legitimately receives both authoritative and uncertain ingests
FilenameParser is preserved as reusable infrastructure, not deleted

The narrow chain-inheritance exception covers a coherent cluster of three type-shaped fields (doc_type, project, authority_scope) that describe what kind of document it is and where it sits in the workflow; version-specific fields (title, version_label, document_date) are correctly excluded as definitionally different across versions, and tags is excluded because it carries set semantics with normal editorial drift
Reading the inherited fields from the predecessor is a graph-state operation that depends on chain context only SAGE owns; it is not pattern matching against caller-defined rules
Mirrors the trust direction established in ADR-019 for edges: SAGE corrects its own prior conclusions but defers to caller/human authority
cons: Requires a coordinated change across schemas, the ingest pipeline, the SAGE MCP toolset, and the CAS application's bulk ingest workflow
Pre-existing entries in the pending_metadata queue need a one-time decision (bulk confirm, bulk archive, or hand-walk) before the new default takes effect

Behavior of vaults with metadata_extraction.review_required=true changes: review now requires explicit needs_review=true on each ingest. During the transition, the CAS application must pass the flag; agents must omit it
FilenameParser becomes a callable library invoked outside the ingest pipeline; an additional round trip is required when the CAS application wants suggestions before commit

adrs.decision: SAGE ingest accepts authoritative values from the caller. IngestRequest gains a needs_review: bool field with default false. When needs_review=false, the ingest pipeline commits caller-supplied values as-is, does not invoke filename inference, and does not set metadata_confirmed=false. When needs_review=true, the document is marked metadata_confirmed=false and appears in the pending_metadata feed for human confirmation; in this mode the pipeline may also invoke filename inference to populate fields the caller did not supply. FilenameParser (sage/services/filename_parser.py) is preserved as a SAGE-provided library and exposed via a new endpoint (POST /parse-filename) and a corresponding MCP tool, both of which return parsed metadata without performing an ingest. One exception is retained inside the ingest pipeline: when IngestRequest.supersedes_document_id is present, the pipeline reads the predecessor's doc_type, project, and authority_scope, and for each of these three fields applies the predecessor's value to the new document if and only if the caller did not supply a value. Caller-supplied values continue to win on a per-field basis. The exception is scoped to these three type-shaped fields. Version-specific fields (title, version_label, document_date) are not inherited because they are definitionally different across versions. tags is excluded from automatic inheritance because it carries set semantics and editorial drift across a chain is normal; callers that want predecessor tags carried forward must do so deliberately. Further expansion of chain inheritance is deferred until a concrete need surfaces. The vault config option metadata_extraction.review_required is deprecated. Once the CAS application's bulk ingest workflow is updated to pass needs_review=true explicitly, the field is removed from vault config schemas and the auto-set behavior is removed from the ingest pipeline.
adrs.rationale: The decision rests on a clean separation of authority. SAGE is the substrate for graph state; callers are the authority for caller-side opinions. Filename heuristics are caller-side opinions: a pattern like 'PV codes map to patent_draft' is a domain choice for a particular workflow, not a property of the substrate. Embedding those rules inside SAGE's ingest pipeline forces SAGE to speak for callers who already have authoritative metadata, which produced both observed symptoms. The narrow chain-inheritance exception covers a coherent cluster of three type-shaped fields -- doc_type, project, authority_scope -- that share a common property: each describes the kind of document or where it sits in the workflow rather than which version it is, and each is typically stable across a supersedes chain. Reading these fields from the predecessor at ingest is a graph-state operation that depends on chain context only SAGE owns; it is not pattern matching against caller-defined rules. Explicit caller-supplied values still take precedence on a per-field basis, which preserves the caller's authoritative role for cases where a chain transition legitimately changes one of these values. The exclusion of title, version_label, and document_date follows directly from the same reasoning: these fields are version-specific by nature. The exclusion of tags is principled rather than arbitrary: tags carry set semantics with normal editorial drift across a chain, and inherit has no unambiguous default (union, replace, or skip), so the field is left to deliberate caller action. The per-call needs_review flag is preferred over a per-vault default because the same vault legitimately receives both kinds of ingests. The pim_health vault sees authoritative agent ingests through the SAGE MCP toolset and uncertain human-driven bulk uploads through the CAS application; the choice of whether to enqueue for review is a property of the call, not the vault. Default false (rather than default true with explicit opt-out) reflects the empirical pattern: the dominant ingest source today is agents calling with authoritative metadata; bulk-ingest review is the minority case and the call site that needs it (CAS app bulk ingest) is a single, known consumer that can be updated to pass the flag explicitly. The trust direction established by ADR-019 for edges (engine corrects its own prior conclusions; humans correct the engine; engine never silently corrects humans) extends here to metadata: SAGE may inherit type-shaped fields from a predecessor it has direct chain knowledge of, but it does not silently overwrite caller-supplied values with inferences derived from caller-defined patterns.
consequences: IngestRequest gains needs_review: bool with default false. Schema change in docs/fs/sage/; manifest version bump; Pydantic regen in sage/models/schemas.py per principle 8.

sage/services/ingestion.py: filename inference (_parse_source_filename and the apply step) and the metadata_confirmed=false setter are gated on needs_review=true. The default path commits caller-supplied metadata as-is and leaves metadata_confirmed at its default (true).

sage/services/ingestion.py: when IngestRequest.supersedes_document_id is set, the pipeline reads the predecessor's doc_type, project, and authority_scope. For each of these three fields, if the caller did not supply a value, the predecessor's value is applied to the new document before any vault default. Caller-supplied values continue to win on a per-field basis (e.g., omitting doc_type while supplying project triggers inheritance of doc_type only).

New endpoint POST /parse-filename and corresponding MCP tool exposure of FilenameParser. Returns parsed metadata (project, codes, title, version, date, doc_type) without performing an ingest. FilenameParser logic is unchanged; only the entry point is new.

sage/sage_api_tools.py and sage/mcp_server.py: sage_ingest tool docstring is updated to document the contract -- agents calling SAGE directly should pass complete metadata and leave needs_review at its default (false); needs_review=true is for callers (notably the CAS application's bulk ingest workflow) that intend the document to be held for human confirmation.

sage/api/routers/ingestion.py and sage/api/routers/pending_metadata.py: route handlers carry the new field through; pending_metadata response shape is unchanged but is populated only when callers opt in via needs_review=true.

Existing entries in pending_metadata at the time of the migration require a one-time decision per vault: bulk-confirm in place, bulk-archive, or hand-walk. The decision is recorded in the project tracker, not this ADR.

Vault config: metadata_extraction.review_required is deprecated. The pim_health vault config retains the field during the transition but the ingest pipeline ignores it once needs_review is wired through. The field and the supporting code path are removed in a cleanup commit after the CAS application is updated to pass needs_review=true on bulk-ingest calls.

CAS application bulk ingest workflow: call parse_filename to obtain suggestions, present to the human for confirmation or edit, then call sage_ingest with the confirmed metadata. The application chooses between needs_review=true (if a second-look review queue is desired even after in-line confirmation) and needs_review=false (if the in-line confirmation is the authoritative step). The default path is the latter; the former is available for cautious workflows.

Agent ingest pattern stabilizes as: pass complete metadata at ingest, omit needs_review (default false). The earlier proposed three-step pattern (ingest, set metadata, review edges) collapses to two steps for the chain-extension common case because chain inheritance fills doc_type, project, and authority_scope when omitted.

ADR-020 (descriptive abstraction prompt with doc_type parameter) interacts positively: chain inheritance produces a correct doc_type at ingest, which is then threaded into the abstraction prompt. Prior to chain inheritance, an incorrectly inferred doc_type would have shaped the abstract incorrectly.

Test coverage: ingest with needs_review=false skips the queue and commits caller values; ingest with needs_review=true marks metadata_confirmed=false and invokes filename inference; chain inheritance fires for doc_type, project, and authority_scope when supersedes_document_id is set and the corresponding field is omitted; per-field independence is preserved (one field can be inherited while another is caller-supplied); explicit caller-supplied values win over chain inheritance on a per-field basis; parse_filename endpoint returns parsed metadata without side effects.

Future expansion of chain inheritance beyond the type-shaped trio inherits this ADR's rationale: the field must be one whose authoritative value is recoverable from chain context (graph state SAGE owns) rather than derived from caller-defined patterns or version-specific by nature. tags would require a separate decision on inheritance semantics (union, replace, skip) before being added; pattern-derived and version-specific fields remain caller-side concerns.

All CAS documentation is currently stale and will be updated as part of post-beta consolidation. The canonical documents named in 'affects' (SAGE Architecture Reference, Formal Substrate) will be revised at that time. Until consolidation, this ADR is the authoritative record of the decision and its rationale.
